analysis.one_liner: Bars the IRS from collecting donors' names and addresses from tax-exempt groups' annual returns.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Tim Scott with 16 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change tax law so the IRS could no longer require tax-exempt organizations — including groups like 501(c)(4) social-welfare organizations that spend heavily on politics — to report the names and addresses of their contributors on their annual returns. Supporters framed it as protecting donors from government targeting after the 2013 IRS controversy over conservative groups. Opponents of such measures say removing donor reporting from IRS filings makes it easier for big donors to fund political advocacy through tax-exempt groups without anyone knowing who is behind the money. The bill got a Senate introduction and a committee referral and nothing more.
analysis.who_benefits: Large donors to politically active tax-exempt organizations. Under current law, such groups must file a schedule listing major contributors with the IRS (not with the general public, though the IRS and, in some cases, courts can see it). Stripping that requirement would let a wealthy individual or corporation fund a political advocacy group with no listing of its support anywhere on the group's filings. Mainstream charities that fear harassment of their donors would also gain a protection they have long sought.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large donors to political tax-exempt groups

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends Internal Revenue Code section 6033 to prohibit the Treasury Secretary from requiring a 501(c) organization to include the name, address, or other identifying information of any contributor, of any amount, on its annual return [S2] [S3].

It keeps narrow exceptions: disclosures required for prohibited tax shelter transactions, and contributions from the organization's own officers, directors, or five highest-paid employees — the people whose pay the public can already see on the return [S2] [S3].

For charity donors without political motives, it removes the risk that their names sit in a federal file that could be exposed by a leak, a data breach, or a future administration's targeting of donors to unpopular causes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Voters, journalists, and watchdog groups lose a paper trail. If a 501(c)(4) or similar group spends millions influencing an election-year debate, no filing would show whose money did it. The IRS also loses one of its tools for verifying that a group claiming a tax exemption — and its funders claiming deductions — is doing what the tax code requires.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters and IRS oversight of exempt groups

drawbacks.text: The bill covers every kind of 501(c) organization, not just charities — including 501(c)(4) social-welfare groups and 501(c)(6) trade associations that routinely spend large sums on political advocacy. Stripping contributor reporting from those groups' returns would make it substantially harder to trace who is financing election-adjacent spending, since the bill applies to contributions of any amount [S2] [S3].

It removes an enforcement tool, not just a disclosure: contributor information is how the IRS checks whether a group's spending matches its claimed tax-exempt purpose, and whether funders are improperly deducting political spending as charity. The bill's own exceptions show the drafting problem — it carves out only the group's own officers and top employees, while the transparency problem involves outside funders [S2] [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: donor privacy genuinely protects small donors and charities from harassment (the historical concern behind donor-list confidentiality), but a blanket federal bar on collecting contributor identities buys that privacy at the cost of accountability for politically active tax-exempt money [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy benefit is real for ordinary charity donors, but the bill draws no line between a soup kitchen and a political advocacy operation: the same blanket prohibition shields both. The heaviest users of the change would be the biggest funders of political tax-exempt groups, and the main cost — losing the ability to see who bankrolls politically active 501(c) organizations — falls on the public. A narrower bill limited to charities would have presented a much fairer trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 14, 2016, and no further action of any kind was taken before the 114th Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Scott introduced the bill on June 14, 2016, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
Sixteen Republican senators cosponsored the bill — all of the bill's support in the record came from one party [S4].
The Finance Committee, chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch, never took the bill up: the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S5].
Because the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without any further action, the bill died in committee and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing reporting rule survived untouched, so transparency advocates and watchdog groups are better off than if it had passed; the bill's backers gained nothing but the introduction itself.

for.name: Sen. Tim Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Sen. Orrin Hatch)
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled action
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on arrival and never held a hearing or markup; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans (the sponsor plus 16 of the chamber's 54 Republicans), and no Democrat or Independent signed on; the bill drew no floor votes, so its only recorded partisan shape is in its sponsorship.

industries.industry: Politically active 501(c) advocacy groups (social-welfare and trade associations)
industries.note: The bill would let these groups accept unlimited funding with no contributor listing on their IRS filings, keeping the source of political spending invisible. Their gain in anonymity is the public's loss of the only paper trail showing who bankrolls their campaigns.

Wealthy funders could route money to politically active tax-exempt groups without their names appearing on any filing the IRS collects. The public cost is not knowing who is paying for the advocacy aimed at them.

Ordinary charity donors gain privacy protection from leaks or politically motivated targeting of donor lists. But the bill offers them the same blanket rule it offers political advocacy groups, so most of the practical change would come where the money is biggest and most political.
